solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: One caught sporting an erection? Carry on!

blocks.note: one is 'a', the indefinite article
ct is a scoring abbreviation for caught in cricket
a man sporting an erection is, in slang, up

explanation.surface: Someone caught in public with an erection is told, Carry On film style, to stop misbehaving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carry on!' reads as a nod to the saucy Carry On films, but it is the definition: to carry on is to misbehave.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry on means to behave badly or make a fuss, which is exactly what it means to ACT UP.

clue.text: Dogs missing bollocks initially – might they be frozen?

indicators.note: initially points to the very start of a word, so only its opening letter is used
something missing is absent, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: bassets are short-legged hounds
the first letter of the rude word

explanation.surface: A vet wonders whether castrated dogs might feel the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the first letter of the rude word from BASSETS to leave ASSETS; the surface makes 'missing bollocks' sound like neutering.
explanation.definitionFit: Governments and courts freeze bank accounts and property, so ASSETS are things that can be frozen; a definition by example.

clue.text: Swinger's equipment: it gets member up with ease, apparently

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means reading from the bottom, so letters run backwards
apparently means as it appears to the ear, so we keep the sound but not the spelling

blocks.note: a member is a part of a body or whole
EZE is said just like the word for comfort

explanation.surface: A sly description of kit for swingers that helps a member rise easily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swinger' and 'member' push a sexual reading; the swinger is an acrobat and the member is a part.
explanation.definitionFit: A trapeze artist swings through the air on a bar hung from ropes, which is the apparatus a circus swinger uses.

clue.text: What Trump supporters claim to be (it's represented with cap embracing insurrection)

definitions.text: What Trump supporters claim to be

indicators.note: to represent something is to present it anew, so the letters are set out in a new order
to embrace is to wrap one's arms around, so one set of letters goes around another

blocks.note: taken as written, the 's read as 'is' and so not part of the letters
taken as written
a riot is a violent uprising

explanation.surface: A dig at the MAGA-capped Capitol rioters who called themselves patriots.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes the red MAGA cap and the January 6 storming of the Capitol, but 'cap' is just letters for the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Trump's supporters describe themselves as loving their country and defending it, which is being PATRIOTIC.

clue.text: Bloody Bill has healed, having trapped end of balls

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept
something trapped is held inside, so one letter sits within the rest

blocks.note: AC is short for account, a bill
healed and cured mean the same
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A man called Bill is recovering after an injury to the testicles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name but is an account, AC. 'Bloody' is a mild British curse word, which is why it can mean damned.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloody, used as an expletive, and accursed both mean damned or wretched, so the words are synonyms.

clue.text: A big enticement to break up PM's 'work get-together'?

indicators.note: breaking something up smashes it to pieces, which can be put back together differently

blocks.note: all fourteen letters as written

explanation.surface: A dig at Downing Street parties during lockdown being passed off as work events.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks recall Partygate, when Boris Johnson's lockdown parties were described as work gatherings; the cabinet is the PM's team of senior ministers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Prime Minister's formal gathering with senior ministers to do government business is literally a work meeting of that group.

clue.text: Desires Stalinist actions to get rid of leader

indicators.note: getting rid of the leader removes whoever stands at the front, so the opening letter goes

blocks.note: Stalin's purges removed his opponents en masse

explanation.surface: A dictator wants to wipe out his rivals, starting at the top.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits Stalin eliminating a leader, but the leader removed is just the first letter of PURGES.
explanation.definitionFit: As nouns, desires and urges are both strong wants or cravings, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Swell working as a theatre performer

blocks.note: a swell of the sea is a surge
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: A dandy is making a fine living on the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' tempts as a posh person and 'theatre' as the stage, but the theatre is an operating theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgeon does their work in a hospital operating theatre, so they perform operations there; a cryptic sense of performer.

clue.text: Condescended to welcome Starmer's no.1, as planned

indicators.note: number one is the first in line, so only the opening letter is used
welcoming a guest means letting them in, so one letter goes inside the others

blocks.note: to deign is to condescend
the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: Someone graciously greets the Labour leader, Keir Starmer, just as arranged.
explanation.walkthrough: Starmer is here only for his initial, slotted inside DEIGNED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something designed has been worked out in advance with intent, so it has been planned; a synonym.

clue.text: UFOs, eh? So unlikely to abduct boorish lot of MPs

indicators.note: an unlikely version is an improbable one, so the letters take a less obvious order
to abduct is to carry someone off inside, so one piece is taken within another

blocks.note: the letters as written
common means vulgar or boorish

explanation.surface: A joke that even aliens would not want to kidnap boorish MPs.
explanation.walkthrough: The UFOs and abduction are pure scenery: 'UFOs, eh? So' is the letter supply.
explanation.definitionFit: The elected chamber of the UK Parliament is where the whole body of MPs sits, making it the collective name for them.

clue.text: Surgically devastating device makes prick flop

blocks.note: a prick stings, and to sting is to smart
a show that flops bombs

explanation.surface: Castration surgery that leaves a man's penis limp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prick' and 'flop' push a rude reading; they are a sting and a failure. 'Surgically' refers to the precision of 'surgical strikes'.
explanation.definitionFit: A guided weapon aimed precisely at a target is used for surgical strikes, so it destroys with surgical accuracy.

clue.text: Misses reverse gear (extremely listless)

indicators.note: to reverse is to go backwards, so the letters run the other way
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outer letters are kept

blocks.note: a rig is a set of equipment or gear
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A lethargic driver keeps failing to find reverse gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Misses' looks like a verb about missing gears; it is the plural of Miss, young women.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss is the title for an unmarried young woman, so misses are young women or girls.

clue.text: Article by ex-PM's missing tons – couldn't be any worse

definitions.note: a phrase describing the state, where the answer is a noun phrase for it

indicators.note: something missing has gone, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: the definite article
Pitt the Elder and the Younger were both British prime ministers
T is the abbreviation for tons

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece by a former prime minister is so thin on substance that it could not be worse.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop one T from THE PITT'S; the surface suggests a heavyweight article missing its heft.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling something the pits is an informal idiom for the very worst situation imaginable, one that could not be worse.

clue.text: Funds, say, invested in fancy Gents

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it, so one piece is placed within another
fancy means elaborate or ornamental, so the letters are dressed up in a new order

blocks.note: e.g. means for example, as does say
taken as written

explanation.surface: Money is spent on a luxury gentlemen's lavatory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invested' is a financial word that fits 'Funds' but here only signals insertion. 'Gents' is British for a men's public toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A nest egg is a sum of money saved up for the future, so it is a reserve of funds.

clue.text: Plant tree casually in arse? Almost

indicators.note: done casually means done carelessly, so the letters fall in no set order
almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
in places one thing inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
booty is slang for the buttocks

explanation.surface: A crude gardening instruction to shove a tree somewhere unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like an instruction to put something in the ground, but it is the definition. 'Almost' works on the slang word for the backside, not on the whole clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Beetroot is a vegetable grown for its dark red root, so it is a kind of plant; a definition by example.

clue.text: On the one occasion in which you texted 'catty thing'

indicators.note: in which says one thing sits inside the other

blocks.note: once means on one occasion
U is text-speak for you

explanation.surface: Someone once sent you a spiteful message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catty' suggests spitefulness, but here it means cat-like: the ounce is the snow leopard.
explanation.definitionFit: The ounce is another name for the snow leopard, a big cat of Central Asia, so literally a cat-like thing.

clue.text: Poetry covered by first two parts of Oxford edition – can't get enough of it

indicators.note: something covered by another is wrapped inside it

blocks.note: verse is poetry
the opening pair of letters of the city name
ed. is the abbreviation for edition

explanation.surface: A reader devours an Oxford edition of poetry and cannot get enough of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The bookish surface hides a racy answer: 'it' is sex, not poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone oversexed has an excessive sexual appetite, so they are never satisfied with the amount they have; 'it' is a coy word for sex.

clue.text: Fantastic place down under  – moving in at last

indicators.note: things that are moving shift position, so the letters change places

blocks.note: the letters as written

explanation.surface: Someone is finally moving into a wonderful new home in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down under' says Australia, but here it means under the sea; 'fantastic' means imaginary, not just wonderful.
explanation.definitionFit: Atlantis is a legendary island said to have sunk beneath the ocean, a fictional location now lying underwater.

clue.text: Helmet on Conservative subject

indicators.note: on means placed against or next to, so one piece is joined to the next

blocks.note: a topi is a sun helmet, the pith helmet of colonial days
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A Tory politician is wearing a helmet, or a helmet is the talking point.
explanation.walkthrough: A topi (or topee) is a lightweight pith helmet once worn in the tropics; a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic is the matter under discussion in a talk or essay, a direct synonym for subject.

clue.text: Lobby to get into photo, like a dick

indicators.note: getting into something means going inside it

blocks.note: pic is short for picture
a hall is an entrance lobby

explanation.surface: A campaigner pushes into a photo and acts like an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lobby' reads as a verb about pressure groups; it is the noun, a hallway. 'Dick' is both an idiot and a penis.
explanation.definitionFit: Phallic means resembling or symbolising the penis, and dick is slang for penis, so like a dick is a fair paraphrase.

clue.text: Muscle men, cynical, but showing compassion

indicators.note: showing means on display, so the letters can be seen in the text

blocks.note: the letters run across these words

explanation.surface: Hardened, cynical bodybuilders unexpectedly reveal a caring side.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignore the punctuation and spaces: the answer runs from the end of 'Muscle' into the start of 'cynical'.
explanation.definitionFit: Clemency is mercy or leniency toward someone who could be punished, which is a form of compassion.

clue.text: Numerous debts after Conservative leader at work!

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is taken
after means following, so one piece comes behind another

blocks.note: the opening letter of the party name
op. is short for opus, a work
an IOU is a written acknowledgement of a debt

explanation.surface: A dig at the Tory leader, who has run up many debts in office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Numerous' looks like it describes the debts, but it stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Copious means plentiful or in large quantity, so a copious supply is a numerous one.

clue.text: Secret police's unchanging state

blocks.note: the Stasi was East Germany's secret police
the possessive ending kept as a letter

explanation.surface: The frozen, repressive state that a secret police force maintains.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the possessive literally: STASI plus its S. The surface apt too, since East Germany under the Stasi was notoriously stagnant.
explanation.definitionFit: Stasis is a condition of balance or inactivity in which nothing moves or develops, a period with no change.

clue.text: Harry penetrates a sheep, which is rather mixed up

indicators.note: to penetrate is to go into something, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: 'a' as written plus a ram, a male sheep
to harry someone is to pester or nag them

explanation.surface: A lurid tabloid tale of a man called Harry and a sheep, which is rather confused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' looks like a name (even a Prince); it is the verb meaning to pester. The definition is self-referential: 'Harry' can be jumbled into 'rather'.
explanation.definitionFit: An anagram is a word whose letters have been rearranged, so it is literally something jumbled; 'rather' being one of 'Harry' makes the joke.

clue.text: Faction of Labour is enduring having relinquished seats?

indicators.note: a faction is a part of a larger body, so the answer is a piece of the text

blocks.note: the letters run across these words

explanation.surface: A Labour faction clings on after the party lost seats at an election.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seats' suggests Parliamentary seats lost at an election; the definition means people who have got up out of their chairs.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has risen has stood up, leaving their chair behind, a playful literal reading of giving up seats.

clue.text: Boozer turned on Mark, another boozer

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so its letters run backwards
on means placed next to, so one piece is joined to the next

blocks.note: a sot is a drunkard
a spot is a mark or stain

explanation.surface: A drunk turns on his drinking companion, a man called Mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a name; it is a spot. A tosspot is an old word for a drunkard, now also British slang for an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: A tosspot is a habitual heavy drinker, so it is a second word for someone who drinks too much.

clue.text: At first Truss lies about the ones trodden underfoot?

indicators.note: at first points to the very beginning, so only the opening letter is used
about can mean around in a jumble, so the letters are moved round

blocks.note: the opening letter of the name
taken as written

explanation.surface: Liz Truss, the briefly serving prime minister, lies about the ordinary people she tramples on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The ones trodden underfoot' reads as the downtrodden masses; the setter means floor tiles.
explanation.definitionFit: Floor tiles are laid on the ground and walked over all day, so they are literally things stepped on.

clue.text: So inbox is tampered with (nothing against university in it) – disgusting

indicators.note: something tampered with has been interfered with, so its letters are disturbed
against means right up next to, so one piece sits beside another
in it says the pair goes inside what came before

blocks.note: the letters as written
nothing is zero, O
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Someone has been meddling with an email inbox, which is revolting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Against' does not mean V here: it just sets O and U side by side before they go inside the shuffled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Obnoxious means extremely unpleasant or offensive, so it is a close synonym for disgusting.

clue.text: As it was written: 'a thousand head' getting BSE?

blocks.note: sic is Latin for thus, used to show a quotation is copied exactly
K stands for a thousand
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: A report of a thousand head of cattle catching mad cow disease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' reads as head of cattle, but it is a headland, NESS, as in Loch Ness country. The question mark flags definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: BSE, bovine spongiform encephalopathy or mad cow disease, is an illness of cattle, an example of an illness.

clue.text: Show no respect towards Charles's top society circles

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: to dis someone is slang for disrespecting them
the opening letter of the name
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: Someone snubs King Charles's upper-class social set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top society circles' reads as high society; 'circles' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A disc is a flat round shape, so discs are circles in the geometric sense; a straightforward synonym.
